la:verb:coarto.gloss: to press together, compress, contract, confine
senses: to press together, compress, contract, confine
la:verb:coarto.html:
cŏ-arto (cŏarcto), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to press together, compress, contract, confine (opp. laxo, dilato, etc.; class.).
Prop.: faenum in struem,; : alveum Tiberis (opp. laxo),: angustae fauces coartant iter,; so : viam,: forum,; : os et fauces sudario, to strangle one's self, : Gnaeus in oppidis coartatus,: in terra,.—
Trop.
Of time, to abridge, shorten: tempus sponsas habendi,: consulatus aliorum,: nox coartat iter,: tempus potestatis censoriae,.—
Of discourse, to abridge, compress: ut Crassus haec quae coartavit et peranguste refersit in oratione suā, dilatet nobis atque explicet,; cf.: plura in unum librum,.—
( = cogo.) To compel, constrain: aliquem ad solutionem debiti, Cod. Th. 2, 29, 2; ; cf.: coarctor e duobus,pressed, urged,.

Trop., that which holds or binds together, a bond, tie (only anteand post-class. and rare): hoc (vinum) continet coagulum convivia, Varr. ap. : animi atque amoris,: amicitiae, Publ. Syr. 27: omnium aerumnarum, i. e. causa,.

senses: to amass, collect or gather together
la:verb:coacervo.html:
cŏ-ăcervo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to heap together, heap up, collect in a mass (class., esp. in prose; most freq. in Cic.).
Prop.: pecuniae coguntur et coacervantur,; cf. : quantum (argenti, etc.) in turbā et rapinis coacervari unā in domo potuit,: tantam vim emblematum,: multitudinem civium,, § 148: cadavera,; cf.: hostium cumulos,: armorum cumulos,: omnis res aliquo, Auct. B. Afr. 91: bustum, * : summas,.—Sarcastically: agros non modo emere verum etiam coacervare, not merely to purchase (perh. to sell again), but to heap, collect together in a mass, Orell.—
Trop.: argumenta,: luctus, * : errores,.

senses: to prove, demonstrate, show, establish, expose
la:verb:coarguo.html:
cŏ-argŭo, ŭi, 3, v. a., orig.,
to assail a person or thing in different directions (cf. arguo init.); hence, jurid. t. t.
Aliquem, to overwhelm with reasoning, refute, silence, expose; convict of guilt or crime, prove guilty (class., most freq. in Cic.; syn. convinco): Graecus testis... vinci, refelli, coargui putat esse turpissimum,: criminibus coarguitur,: ut illum natura ipsius consuetudoque defendat, hunc autem haec cadem coarguant,: decreto,: Lentulum dissimulantem coarguunt praeter litteras sermonibus, etc.,: Libonem in senatu,: in exprobrando et coarguendo acer (gestus),—With gen. of the crime: aliquem avaritiae,: commutati indicii,: sceleris,: facinoris .—
Aliquid, to prove incontestably a crime, a wrong, a fallacy, etc., to demonstrate or show to be wrong, to refute (cf. arguo, II.): sin autem fuga laboris desidiam coarguit, nimirum, etc.,: rem certioribus argumentis,: certum crimen multis suspitionibus,: errorem,: perfidiam,: mendacium,: Lacedaemoniorum tyrannidem,: temeritatem artis,: vitia,: iniquitatem,: quam (legem) usus coarguit,which experience has proved to be injudicious,; cf. : quod coarguunt fici,disprove,: domini coarguit aures,betrays, publishes, makes known, (cf. arguo, II. fin.).—With a clause as object: quod falsum esse pluribus coarguitur,; Auct. B. Alex. 68.

la:verb:coaequo.html:
cŏ-aequo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.,
to make one thing equal or even with another, to even, level (rare but in good prose).
Prop.: aream, and 129: montes,: pastinatum,: sulcum,: glaebas,; cf. —
Trop.
To make equal in worth, dignity, power, etc., to bring to the same level, place on the same footing, equalize: ad libidines injuriasque tuas omnia coaequasti, * : gratiam omnium,: coaequati dignitate, pecuniā, virtute, etc.,: primogenito tuo,: pedes meos cervis,.—
To compare (late Lat.): aliquem cum aliquo, Lact. de Ira Dei, 7: aliquem alicui,.

la:verb:coangusto.html:
cŏ-angusto, āvi, ātum, v. a.,
to bring into a narrow compass, to confine, compress, contract, enclose, hem in (rare and mostly post-Aug.).
Prop.: alvos, * : quo facilius fistula claudatur vel certe coangustetur,; Auct. B. Hisp. 5; cf. : aditum aedium,.—Of a city, to invest, besiege: et coangustabunt te undique,.—
Trop., to limit, restrict: haec lex dilatata in ordinem cunctum, coangustari etiam potest, * : aliquid interpretatione,.—
In gen., to afflict, .

la:verb:coacesco.html:
cŏ-ăcesco, ăcŭi, 3,
v. inch. n., to become acid or sour (rare but in good prose).
Prop.: genus uvae,; cf.: ut non omne vinum, sic non omnis aetas vetustate coacescit,; pr.: secunda mensa in imbecillo stomacho coacescit,: si coacuit intus cibus aut computruit, —
Trop (the fig. drawn from wine): quare cum integri nihil fuerit in hac gente plenā, quam valde eam putamus tot transfusionibus coacuisse? to deteriorate or become corrupt, B. and K.; cf. supra.
